hook: The scientist who turned a telescope on the sky and stood trial for saying the Earth moves.

pages.x: Galileo Galilei was born in Pisa in 1564, the son of a musician. He began studying medicine, then fell in love with mathematics. A story says that, watching a lamp swing in Pisa cathedral, he timed it with his pulse and found that every swing took the same time, big or small.
He rolled balls down ramps and found that falling things speed up at a steady rate, and that without air, heavy and light objects fall equally fast.
pages.fx: He proved Aristotle wrong, and laid the foundations for Newton's laws of motion.

pages.x: In 1609 he built a telescope that magnified 20 times, and saw mountains on the Moon, the countless stars of the Milky Way, four moons circling Jupiter and the phases of Venus.
pages.fx: They showed that not everything circles the Earth, strong evidence for Copernicus, and astronomy has used telescopes ever since.

pages.x: He published his discoveries in 1610 in a little book, The Starry Messenger, and named the moons of Jupiter after the Medici, who made him their court mathematician in Florence. He became famous across Europe.

In 1632 he published the Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems. In it, the character who defends the Earth-centred universe, named Simplicio, sounds like a fool, and uses an argument of the pope himself.
pages.img: Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems

pages.x: In 1633 the Inquisition put him on trial in Rome. Threatened with torture, aged 69, he knelt and declared that the Earth does not move. A legend says he muttered as he got up: "And yet it moves." He spent his last eight years under house arrest, going blind.
In 1992 Pope John Paul II admitted the Church had been wrong to condemn him. The middle finger of his right hand, cut off when his body was moved in 1737, is on show in a museum in Florence.
Galileo is called the father of modern science for testing ideas by experiment and measurement. Einstein called him the father of modern physics, and NASA named a spacecraft to Jupiter after him.
pts: Defended the Sun-centred system against the Church
